strengths: MultiBanana addresses a useful computer-vision evaluation problem: preserving and composing information from heterogeneous reference images. Its 3,769 tasks, including 2,598 multi-reference tasks with 3–8 references, substantially extend the coverage of the closest benchmarks discussed in the paper.

The dataset goes beyond reference count by annotating cross-domain combinations, scale/viewpoint differences, rare concepts, and multilingual text. These dimensions offer potentially useful diagnostics for applications where simple subject composition is insufficient.

The construction pipeline combines automatic filtering with manual verification. Appendix A provides concrete filtering thresholds, synthetic-image generation categories, and task-construction procedures, while the supplementary material supplies evaluator prompts and detailed results.

Evaluation of five generators, two VLM judges, and several iterative generation strategies provides substantial empirical coverage. The qualitative examples illustrate practically relevant failures, including subject omission, incorrect text, and inconsistent composition. Reporting that agentic refinement can degrade Nano Banana's performance is also informative.
weaknesses: The principal concern is evaluation validity. Appendix G.2 explicitly couples the supposedly independent criteria: instruction alignment is capped at 6 for unnatural appearance even when instructions are followed correctly, while compositing artifacts also lower background match, physical realism, and visual quality. Reference consistency demands preservation of fine details without explicitly exempting attributes that the instruction asks to change. Background matching penalizes stylistic differences from references, potentially conflicting with cross-domain composition or requested style transfer. These rules can penalize valid edits and make the claimed fidelity–quality trade-off difficult to interpret.

No human validation of the proposed scoring protocol is reported. Appendix D instead measures agreement between GPT and Gemini, obtaining correlations of 0.549–0.650, and checks whether an improved Qwen model receives higher scores. These are useful sanity checks but do not establish that the rubric measures human judgments correctly on these unusually heterogeneous tasks. This matters especially because the same model families generate synthetic references, construct tasks, judge outputs, and supply the strongest evaluated generators. Averaging two judges does not independently establish freedom from shared biases.

The analyses do not isolate the proposed difficulty factors. Figure 6 compares samples containing a factor with all other samples, without matching reference count, task type, synthetic-image provenance, or overlapping difficulty labels. Consequently, lower scores establish associations rather than the independent effects suggested by the 'orthogonal axes' framing. Likewise, the rubric assigns instruction alignment a score of 1 whenever any required subject is missing, so increasing reference count mechanically increases opportunities for score collapse even at unchanged per-subject accuracy. Per-reference measurements would help distinguish this effect from declining integration capability.

Reproducibility and comparison fairness remain incomplete despite the extensive supplement. Generator inference settings, input resizing/packing, sampling repetitions, and failure handling are not sufficiently specified. Table 3 aggregates OmniGen2 over fewer reference counts than other models, so its multi-reference averages are not directly comparable; moreover, the text says it is evaluated only at five references, whereas Tables 8–10 include three and four. Section 3.1 describes 48 multi-reference task variants, including instruction-free variants, while Table 1 reports 36 total task types, leaving the actual evaluated protocol ambiguous.

Several conclusions exceed the evidence. Appendix C calls earlier benchmarks nearly solved, although Table 5 reports many scores around 0.5–0.78 and even labels the abstract metric with a downward arrow while interpreting larger values as better. The modest agentic improvements lack uncertainty estimates and an equal-budget repeated-generation baseline. These issues are secondary to the scoring concerns, but further weaken the strength of the conclusions. Overall, the dataset has worthwhile value, yet the unresolved validity of its central measurement protocol currently outweighs the case for acceptance.

strengths: MultiBanana addresses a relevant evaluation gap: composing heterogeneous references rather than evaluating only conventional image edits. Its 3,769 tasks, including 2,598 multi-reference tasks with 3–8 inputs, provide useful coverage of reference count, domain differences, scale differences, rare concepts, and multilingual text.

The construction pipeline includes automatic filtering, hierarchical categorization, and manual verification. The supplement provides filtering thresholds, detailed statistics, evaluation prompts, and agent prompts, making substantial parts of the methodology inspectable.

Evaluation of five generators, separate results from two judges, and extensive qualitative examples provide useful diagnostic evidence. The observed subject omissions and compositional failures identify practical limitations of current systems.

The agent experiments report mixed outcomes transparently: prompt refinement improves GPT-Image-1 modestly but does not consistently improve Nano Banana. A benchmark contribution does not require a new state-of-the-art generator.
weaknesses: The central concern is evaluation validity. Appendix G.2 caps Instruction Alignment at 6 for unnatural appearance even when instructions are followed correctly, and penalizes compositing across several purportedly independent dimensions. Reference Consistency demands fine-detail preservation without explicitly exempting instructed changes; Background-Subject Match penalizes even slight style or lighting differences from references. These rules can penalize valid harmonization of heterogeneous references and entangle instruction following with aesthetics, undermining the interpretation of the five scores.

The manuscript provides no direct human validation on this benchmark. Appendix D instead reports judge-to-judge correlations of 0.549–0.650 and a single-reference model-version comparison. These are useful checks, but neither establishes that the judges correctly assess identity preservation, multilingual rendering, or intentional stylization in the proposed difficult settings. This is particularly consequential given the rubric concerns.

The difficulty analyses do not isolate the proposed factors. Figure 6 compares samples containing each condition against other samples without matching reference count, task type, synthetic provenance, or overlapping difficulty labels. Likewise, increasing reference count also increases required content, while the rubric forces Instruction Alignment to 1 if any required subject is absent. The results establish associations, but cannot cleanly distinguish intrinsic reference-handling difficulty from task composition and scoring effects.

Synthetic references are produced by two of the evaluated generators, and Appendix A.1 states that all text-containing synthetic images come from GPT-Image-1. No source-stratified analysis tests whether reference provenance affects rankings or the multilingual conclusions. This is a plausible benchmark bias that remains unmeasured, rather than proof that the rankings are wrong.

Some comparisons and reproducibility details remain unclear. Table 10 evaluates OmniGen2 on 3–5 references, whereas other models cover 3–8; Table 3 therefore compares aggregates over different difficulty distributions. Section 4 also inconsistently describes OmniGen2 as evaluated only at five references. Exact generation settings, repeated-run variability, and uncertainty for the small agent improvements are not reported. Separately, the stated 36 tasks in Table 1 conflict with the 48 multi-reference variants described in Section 3.1.

Overall, the dataset has worthwhile scope and potential usefulness, but the scoring protocol and its insufficient validation affect the benchmark's central scientific conclusions. These substantive concerns outweigh the merits in the submitted version and determine the Weak Reject recommendation; presentation inconsistencies alone would not.

strengths: MultiBanana addresses a useful computer-vision evaluation gap: composing heterogeneous references while preserving subject identity. Extending evaluation to eight references and explicitly labeling domain, scale/viewpoint, rare-concept, and multilingual challenges provides value beyond conventional editing benchmarks.

The dataset represents substantial curation effort: 3,769 tasks, including 2,598 multi-reference tasks, with reasonably balanced reference counts and at least 70 examples per multi-reference task/count combination. Automatic filtering and manual verification are described.

Evaluation spans five open and closed models, with detailed per-task and per-criterion results. Quantitative trends and qualitative examples provide useful evidence of subject omission, composition failures, and difficulty preserving reference details.

The supplement supplies judge and agent prompts, filtering thresholds, separate evaluator results, and three iterative inference baselines. Reporting that refinement sometimes degrades Nano Banana is informative and appropriately acknowledges limitations.
weaknesses: The central scoring protocol lacks direct human validation on this benchmark. Appendix D reports moderate agreement between two VLM judges (overall correlation 0.650), but agreement between automated judges does not establish correctness or human alignment. Detecting improvement between two Qwen versions is also insufficient validation of fine-grained multi-reference judgments. This is consequential because the benchmark's rankings and principal conclusions depend on these scores.

The evaluation rubric can penalize legitimate transformations and entangles supposedly independent criteria. Appendix G.2 caps instruction alignment for unnatural appearance even when instructions are followed, and caps background-subject match for deviations from reference style or lighting. Reference consistency requires fine details to match without explicitly exempting instructed changes. Appendix E.3 itself attributes deductions to domain unification and pose changes made for natural composition. These rules risk conflating successful editing with failure and complicate the claimed fidelity-versus-coherence trade-off.

The difficulty-factor analysis is observational rather than controlled. Figure 6 compares samples containing each factor against all remaining samples without matching reference count, task type, or overlapping difficulty factors. Consequently, score differences do not isolate the contribution of domain mismatch, scale, rarity, or multilingual content. Only 99 tasks contain multilingual references, and uncertainty is not reported for these comparisons.

Benchmark construction introduces an unquantified source-dependence concern: the two evaluated closed models generate synthetic references, and GPT-Image-1 exclusively generates text-containing references (Appendix A.1). No real-versus-synthetic or source-generator breakdown establishes whether relative performance is stable across these sources. This does not demonstrate bias, but leaves an important benchmark-validity question unresolved.

Several reporting issues affect comparability and reproducibility. Table 3 aggregates OmniGen2 over fewer reference counts than other models, without clearly marking that difference in the table; Section 4's claim of evaluation only at five references also conflicts with Tables 8–10. Section 3.1 describes 48 multi-reference tasks including instruction-free variants, whereas Table 1 reports 36 total tasks and instruction-free results are not separately identified. Generation settings and repeated-run uncertainty are insufficiently documented, limiting interpretation of the relatively small agentic improvements.

Overall, the dataset's scope and diagnostic potential are worthwhile, but the unvalidated, potentially conflicting scoring rules and uncontrolled difficulty comparisons weaken its core claim to provide reliable standardized evaluation. These substantive concerns, rather than the absence of a new generation method or minor presentation flaws, place the balance at weak reject.

strengths: MultiBanana addresses a useful computer-vision evaluation problem: composing heterogeneous visual references while preserving subjects and following instructions. Its 3,769 tasks, 36 task types, and support for up to eight references substantially extend the coverage of several existing benchmarks.

The construction pipeline includes meaningful curation: image-quality filtering, synthetic supplementation of underrepresented categories, hierarchical labeling, and manual verification of instructions. Explicit annotations for domain, scale/viewpoint, rare concepts, and multilingual content enable useful diagnostic evaluation.

Experiments cover five open and closed models and provide detailed breakdowns by task, reference count, and scoring dimension. Qualitative examples substantiate the existence of subject omission, compositional artifacts, and text-rendering failures.

The supplementary material adds valuable evaluation infrastructure and checks: explicit judge prompts, cross-judge correlations, repeated-judging stability, an open-weight judge, evaluation costs, synthetic-source analysis, and three agentic baselines.
weaknesses: The central scoring rubric does not cleanly measure the claimed independent dimensions. Appendix J.2 caps Instruction Alignment at 6 for unnatural appearance even when the instruction is followed correctly, while compositing artifacts also reduce several quality scores. Reference Consistency requires fine details to match without explicitly exempting instructed changes, and Background–Subject Match penalizes differences from reference styles even in transformation tasks. These rules risk penalizing valid edits and repeatedly counting the same defect. Because benchmark validity is the main contribution, this is a material concern.

The rubric also complicates the reference-count analysis: omission of any required subject forces Instruction Alignment to 1, and detail errors trigger hard consistency caps. Increasing the number of subjects increases opportunities to trigger these rules even with unchanged per-subject accuracy. Figure 5 therefore establishes declining aggregate task success, but does not isolate declining reference-handling capability. Complementary per-subject retention and fidelity measurements are missing.

Human validation is too limited to resolve these measurement concerns. Section 4.4 uses only 32 samples and three evaluators, without reporting sampling coverage, human–human agreement, per-criterion agreement, or uncertainty. Pearson correlations of 0.55–0.69 are encouraging but do not establish reliable scoring across 36 tasks and up to eight references. Appendix E's judge agreement and repeatability checks demonstrate consistency rather than correctness.

The difficult-factor analysis compares unmatched subsets containing versus lacking each factor (Figure 7). Reference count, task type, synthetic provenance, and overlapping difficulty factors are not controlled, so score differences cannot be attributed specifically to domain, scale, rarity, or language. Likewise, the explanation that closed models distort scenes because they overfit reference details remains a plausible interpretation rather than a demonstrated mechanism.

Some comparison and reproducibility details remain unresolved. Section 4 says OmniGen2 is evaluated only in the five-reference setting, whereas Tables 12–14 report three-, four-, and five-reference results; its Table 3 aggregate consequently does not cover the same reference range as other models. Appendix G leaves code and dataset links blank and omits important generation settings and precise generator versions. These omissions prevent verification of the claimed standardized, reproducible comparison.

The dataset has clear potential value, but the balance currently favors rejection because the main conclusions depend on a scoring protocol whose construct validity is insufficiently established. This concern is more consequential than presentation issues or limited model coverage.

strengths: MultiBanana addresses a useful computer-vision evaluation problem: composing heterogeneous visual references while preserving subject identity and following instructions. Its 3,769 tasks, 36 task types, and support for up to eight references provide substantial coverage beyond the smaller benchmarks compared in Table 1.

The construction pipeline is reasonably detailed, including image filtering thresholds, category balancing, synthetic-reference generation, and human verification. Cross-domain, scale/viewpoint, rare-concept, and multilingual annotations support potentially useful diagnostic evaluations.

Experiments cover five generators, multiple reference counts, and several task structures. The quantitative results and qualitative examples provide evidence of genuine difficulties, including subject omission and poor integration of reference content.

The supplementary material strengthens the evaluation through cross-judge correlations, repeated judging, an accessible open-source judge, source-bias analysis, explicit evaluation prompts, and agentic baselines. These are meaningful efforts toward validating and reproducing the benchmark.
weaknesses: The principal concern is the validity of the scoring rubric (Appendix J.2). Instruction Alignment is capped for unnatural appearance even when instructions are correctly followed, while compositing artifacts are penalized again under several quality dimensions. Reference Consistency demands matching fine details without explicitly exempting attributes the instruction requests changing. Background–Subject Match penalizes even slight stylistic differences from references, which is problematic for heterogeneous-reference tasks. Consequently, the five dimensions are not cleanly separated, and low scores can reflect conflicting rubric requirements rather than generation failures.

Human validation is insufficient to resolve these concerns. Table 4 uses only 32 samples and three evaluators across a benchmark containing 36 task types. Sampling composition, human inter-rater agreement, per-criterion agreement, and uncertainty are not reported. Pearson correlations of 0.57 for Gemini and 0.55 for Qwen provide limited support for the broad reliability claims. The additional cross-VLM and repeatability analyses establish consistency more directly than agreement with human judgments.

The difficult-reference analysis compares each tagged subset against all remaining tasks without controlling for reference count, task type, or overlapping difficulty tags (Figures 7 and 19). These comparisons establish associations but do not isolate the proposed difficulty factors. Furthermore, assigning Instruction Alignment a score of 1 whenever any required subject is absent makes increasing-reference degradation partly sensitive to an all-or-nothing scoring rule; per-subject fulfillment would help distinguish this effect from worsening individual-reference handling.

Several interpretations exceed the evidence. The claim that closed models degrade because they overfit reference details is not established by the aggregate scores and selected examples. Appendix F.4's overlapping 99% confidence intervals do not establish absence of synthetic-source bias, and its analysis lacks a real-reference control. Appendix F.5 claims the non-prioritized criterion is maintained, although Table 15 shows decreases in that criterion under both priority interventions.

Reproducibility and comparison details remain incomplete. Appendix G identifies judge endpoints but omits important generator inference and preprocessing settings. Section 4 says OmniGen2 is evaluated only in the five-reference setting, whereas Table 14 reports three-, four-, and five-reference results; Table 3 compares its restricted-coverage averages with other models evaluated through eight references. This is correctable, but requires clarification. Overall, the dataset has worthwhile potential, yet the unresolved measurement-validity concerns and insufficient human calibration currently outweigh the case for acceptance.

strengths: MultiBanana addresses a useful evaluation gap: composing heterogeneous visual references at increasing reference counts. Its 3,769 tasks, 36 task configurations, and support for up to eight references constitute a substantial benchmark contribution beyond the smaller reference sets in OmniContext and DreamOmni2.

The construction process is systematic: category-aware sampling, explicit filtering thresholds, synthetic supplementation of underrepresented categories, and human verification of instructions. The four challenging reference categories provide useful diagnostic coverage beyond aggregate generation quality.

Experiments cover five relevant open and closed models, with detailed results by task, reference count, and evaluation dimension. The quantitative results and qualitative examples substantiate substantial remaining difficulties, including omitted subjects, identity degradation, and compositional artifacts.

The supplementary material meaningfully strengthens the evaluation through separate judge results, repeated-judgment measurements, an open-weight judge, synthetic-source analysis, and agentic baselines. Publishing the judge and agent prompts also improves methodological transparency.
weaknesses: The central scoring rubric conflates dimensions and can penalize legitimate transformations. Appendix J.2 caps instruction alignment at six for unnatural appearance even when instructions are followed correctly, while compositing artifacts also reduce several quality scores. Reference consistency requires matching fine details without explicitly exempting instructed changes, and background–subject matching penalizes differences from reference styles despite cross-domain and style-transfer tasks. These rules weaken the interpretation of the claimed fidelity–quality trade-off; this is a measurement concern rather than a presentation issue.

Human validation is too limited to establish reliability across the benchmark's heterogeneous tasks. Table 4 uses only 32 samples and three evaluators, without reporting sample coverage, human inter-rater agreement, per-dimension agreement, or uncertainty. Pearson correlations of 0.55–0.69 provide encouraging but incomplete evidence. Cross-VLM correlations and small standard errors of aggregate scores do not establish that judges correctly distinguish instructed transformations from fidelity failures.

The difficulty analysis does not isolate the proposed factors. Figure 7 compares tasks containing each factor with all remaining tasks without matching reference counts, task types, or overlapping difficulty labels. Likewise, reference-count comparisons use different task sets, and the rubric forces instruction alignment to one whenever any required subject is absent. Consequently, the observed declines demonstrate difficulty under this protocol but do not cleanly identify independent effects or establish the proposed causal explanation of overfitting to reference details.

Some supplementary conclusions exceed their evidence. Appendix F.4 compares reference-source subsets only for the two closed generators, which cannot rule out a shared synthetic-reference advantage over open models; overlapping confidence intervals also do not establish equivalence. Table 15 shows that prioritizing consistency reduces background–subject matching from 3.67 to 3.25, while prioritizing matching reduces consistency from 3.58 to 3.40, so the claim of maintaining the other criterion needs qualification.

Reproducibility and comparison details remain incomplete. Generator settings, input preprocessing, failure handling, and sampling protocols are insufficiently specified. OmniGen2 is evaluated over fewer reference counts, making its Table 3 aggregates non-equivalent to other models; the text also inconsistently describes its coverage. Overall, the substantial dataset and diagnostic evidence place the paper near the acceptance boundary, but unresolved validity of its central scoring protocol prevents a stronger recommendation.
